A close reading for the week

“Who are you?”

Alice in Wonderland · Chapter V

A child who has changed size several times before lunch meets a caterpillar who demands to know who she is. The rudest question in Wonderland is also philosophy’s oldest, and for once the child gives the rigorous answer.

The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are you?”1 said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied, rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know who I was when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then.”2

  1. 1

    The stress on “you”

    Carroll’s italics fall on you: the Caterpillar wants to know what she is, never mind her name or business. It is the rudest possible opening, with no greeting, from a stranger three inches high with a hookah, and it is also the book’s deepest question, which Alice has already asked herself in Chapter II: “Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!” Wonderland keeps handing the puzzle back to her, here in its bluntest form.

  2. 2

    Identity given a timetable

    Alice’s answer is scrupulously exact: she knows who she was this morning, but has “been changed several times since then”. For once the child gives the rigorous answer: she will not claim a continuity she cannot verify. Behind the joke sits a real philosophical problem, as old as the ship of Theseus: what makes a changing thing the same thing? Alice, who has been nine feet tall and three inches small before lunch, has better evidence than most philosophers.
